paras: The threatened lynching of Cornie O'Brien and Warren Murphy took place at Osage, Iowa, in late July and early August 1888, when two youths aged 17 and 15, jailed on a charge of first-degree murder, became the object of 'strong talk of lynching.' They were accused of beating to death Henry Stocum, a 19-year-old orphan, and no attack on them was reported. Midwestern and Plains papers carried the case as an example of youthful violence, and a wire brief about 'threats of lynching the prisoners' ran for more than two weeks.

According to an Osage special telegram to the Omaha Bee, Stocum had caught O'Brien in the act of turning several cans of cream into a well, and the two exchanged words. A few nights later, as Stocum returned from a neighbor's farm where he had been working, he was waylaid by two young men whom he recognized as O'Brien and Murphy, and was beaten badly enough to need a physician. The pair were arrested the next day and tried in a justice court at Riceville, where, in the Bee's words, 'to the surprise of everybody,' they were discharged after paying a fine of $5 and costs.

Stocum died on a Saturday night after lingering a little more than a week. On the following Monday, Sheriff St. John went to Douglas township, ten miles east of Osage, arrested the two boys and charged them with murder in the first degree. The Bee's dispatch, dated August 1, closed: 'Great indignation exists and there is strong talk of lynching.'
A shorter wire brief likewise reported that 'there are threats of lynching the prisoners.' Neither account named who made the threats or described any gathering at the jail.

On August 16 a Minnesota weekly reported the two boys in jail at Osage, in Mitchell County, and added that Stocum had said before dying that he recognized them as his assailants. No report of an indictment, trial or verdict appears in the coverage.

The Omaha Bee ran the fullest account under the headlines 'Kids of Tough Proclivities' and 'Two Boy Murderers at Osage,' pairing it with the arrest of two Des Moines boys for trying to wreck a Rock Island train. The Beatrice Daily Express printed a short wire version that named the dead man 'Henry Slocum' and left out the lynching talk. Several Minnesota weeklies rewrote the Bee story as 'Youthful Roudyism in Iowa,' also without the lynching sentence.

The lynching threat reached readers mainly through a one-paragraph news-summary brief. The Frontier of O'Neill, Nebraska, printed it on August 9 and again on August 16, beside a second brief saying the affair 'grew out of trivial boy differences.' The Custer Chronicle in Dakota ran the threat brief on August 11 and again on August 18, while the Sully County Watchman printed the same paragraph with the threat sentence cut. None of these papers commented on the threats, and none stated the race of anyone involved.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Cornie O'Brien and Warren Murphy
bases: Two youths jailed on a murder charge were the subject of 'strong talk of lynching' and 'threats of lynching the prisoners' (A1, A4, A10); no attack on them was reported.

No one was killed: the coverage reports only talk and threats of lynching the two prisoners over the death of Henry Stocum (A1, A4), and a week later they were still reported in jail at Osage (A11). Who made the threats and how many were involved is not stated.

The arrest on a murder charge is reported in several separately worded items (A1, A2, A5, A11), and the lynching talk appears both in the Osage special telegram to the Omaha Bee (A1) and in a differently worded wire brief (A4, A10), though the two may share a source.

framing.detail: The Omaha Bee grouped the case with a train-wrecking attempt under 'Kids of Tough Proclivities' and 'Iowa Furnishes Some Specimens of Youthful Depravity', reporting the lynching talk without comment.
Plains weeklies ran a one-paragraph brief ending 'There are threats of lynching the prisoners,' some twice a week apart.
Minnesota weeklies printed the story as 'Youthful Roudyism in Iowa', dropping the lynching sentence.

conflicts.note: Spelling variants of one name in OCR and wire copy; Stocum is the more frequent form, including in the Osage special (A1).

info: Talk of lynching reported in an Osage dispatch dated August 1, 1888, after the arrest on Monday (July 30) and Stocum's death the previous Saturday night (July 28); the threat brief was still running August 9-18.
Osage, Iowa; the boys were arrested in Douglas township, ten miles east of Osage, and held in jail at Osage.
The prisoners threatened: Cornie (or Carnie) O'Brien, 17, and Warren Murphy, 15. The man whose death they were charged with: Henry Stocum (Stocuin, Slocum), 19, described as an orphan from Brooklyn.

Charged with first-degree murder for waylaying and beating Henry Stocum, who died of his injuries a little more than a week later; the assault was said to follow a quarrel after Stocum found O'Brien turning cans of cream into a well.
Not identified; the coverage speaks only of 'great indignation' and 'strong talk of lynching' and of 'threats of lynching the prisoners'.
As of August 16 the two were reported in jail at Osage; no report of an indictment, trial or verdict was found.
